expectedText:
SMALL ESTATE AFFIDAVIT
Prepared for Pat Morgan · March 15, 2026

SMALL ESTATE DECLARATION
I, Jordan Morgan, declare that Pat Morgan died on March 15, 2026, and that I am the successor of Pat Morgan entitled to collect the property described in the attached schedule under the small estate affidavit procedure of California Probate Code §§ 13100-13106. A certified copy of Pat Morgan's death certificate is attached to this declaration.

THE PERSONAL-PROPERTY SMALL ESTATE THRESHOLD AND 40-DAY WAIT
California Probate Code § 13100 lets a successor of Pat Morgan collect money owed to Pat Morgan, receive Pat Morgan's tangible personal property, or have evidence of a debt, security, or similar right transferred, without procuring letters of administration or awaiting probate of a will, when two things are both true: the gross value of Pat Morgan's real and personal property located in California — after excluding the property categories listed in Probate Code § 13050 — does not exceed $166,250, and at least 40 days have elapsed since March 15, 2026. That $166,250 figure is the amount currently written into the statute, as amended effective January 1, 2025; Probate Code § 890 separately directs the Judicial Council to re-adjust it for inflation every three years, so a different dollar amount can be the one actually operative depending on the decedent's exact date of death.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Excluding the property described in Section 13050 and any property included in a petition filed under Section 13151, if the gross value of the decedent's real and personal property in this state does not exceed one hundred sixty-six thousand two hundred fifty dollars ($166,250), as adjusted periodically in accordance with Section 890, and if 40 days have elapsed since the death of the decedent, the successor of the decedent may, without procuring letters of administration or awaiting probate of the will, do any of the following with respect to one or more particular items of property: (a) Collect any particular item of property that is money due the decedent. (b) Receive any particular item of property that is tangible personal property of the decedent. (c) Have any particular item of property that is evidence of a debt, obligation, interest, right, security, or chose in action belonging to the decedent transferred, whether or not secured by a lien on real property."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13100, California Probate Code, personal-property small estate affidavit threshold and 40-day wait (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13100.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one state's no-probate small-estate collection mechanism — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's estate, and not a statement that any particular estate qualifies. Small-estate thresholds and procedures vary enormously by state; some states have no comparable mechanism at all, and California's own figure is scheduled for further periodic inflation adjustment, so the dollar amount in effect on a particular date of death can differ from the figure quoted here. This is a single statutory section (§ 13100); no additional independent source was found for this.

PROPERTY EXCLUDED FROM THE SMALL-ESTATE CALCULATION
Probate Code § 13050 lists what does not count toward the $166,250 ceiling. Excluded: property Pat Morgan held in joint tenancy, a life estate or other interest that ended at death, property that passed outright to a surviving spouse under § 13500, property in a trust revocable by Pat Morgan during Pat Morgan's lifetime, and a multiple-party (joint or pay-on-death) account, to the extent the funds belong after death to a surviving party or named P.O.D. payee or beneficiary. Also excluded: vehicles registered, or vessels numbered, under the Vehicle Code, and manufactured homes, mobilehomes, commercial coaches, truck campers, and floating homes registered under the Health and Safety Code. Also excluded from the value calculation: any amount owed to Pat Morgan for Armed Forces service, and up to $16,625 of unpaid salary or other compensation (including unused vacation pay) owed to Pat Morgan from employment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) For the purposes of this part: (1) Any property or interest or lien thereon that, at the time of the decedent's death, was held by the decedent as a joint tenant, or in which the decedent had a life or other interest terminable upon the decedent's death, or that was held by the decedent and passed to the decedent's surviving spouse pursuant to Section 13500, shall be excluded in determining the property or estate of the decedent or its value. This excluded property shall include, but not be limited to, property in a trust revocable by the decedent during the decedent's lifetime. (2) A multiple-party account to which the decedent was a party at the time of the decedent's death shall be excluded in determining the property or estate of the decedent or its value, whether or not all or a portion of the sums on deposit are community property, to the extent that the sums on deposit belong after the death of the decedent to a surviving party, P.O.D. payee, or beneficiary. ... (b) For the purposes of this part, all of the following property shall be excluded in determining the property or estate of the decedent or its value: (1) Any vehicle registered under Division 3 (commencing with Section 4000) of the Vehicle Code or titled under Division 16.5 (commencing with Section 38000) of the Vehicle Code. (2) Any vessel numbered under Division 3.5 (commencing with Section 9840) of the Vehicle Code. (3) Any manufactured home, mobilehome, commercial coach, truck camper, or floating home registered under Part 2 (commencing with Section 18000) of Division 13 of the Health and Safety Code. (c) For the purposes of this part, the value of the following property shall be excluded in determining the value of the decedent's property in this state: (1) Any amounts due to the decedent for services in the Armed Forces of the United States. (2) The amount, not exceeding sixteen thousand six hundred twenty-five dollars ($16,625), as adjusted periodically in accordance with Section 890, of salary or other compensation, including compensation for unused vacation, owing to the decedent for personal services from any employment."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13050, California Probate Code, property excluded from the small-estate calculation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13050.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what one state excludes from a small-estate calculation — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's estate. Other states define — and limit — comparable exclusion lists very differently, and property not listed here (most other financial accounts, most personal belongings, and most vehicles outside the specific Vehicle Code categories quoted) still counts toward the ceiling. This is a single statutory section (§ 13050); no additional independent source was found for this.

THE 40-DAY WAITING PERIOD, PRECISELY
The personal-property small-estate procedure is unavailable until 40 days have elapsed after Pat Morgan's death on March 15, 2026: Probate Code § 13100 makes the entire procedure conditional on that 40-day elapse, and § 13101(a)(3) separately requires the affidavit or declaration itself to state that at least 40 days have elapsed, as shown by the certified copy of the death certificate attached to it. This 40-day figure applies only to the personal-property affidavit — the separate real-property affidavit under § 13200 instead requires six months to elapse.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "and if 40 days have elapsed since the death of the decedent, the successor of the decedent may, without procuring letters of administration or awaiting probate of the will, do any of the following with respect to one or more particular items of property"
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13100, California Probate Code, 40-day condition on the procedure's availability (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13100.)
  ""At least 40 days have elapsed since the death of the decedent, as shown in a certified copy of the decedent's death certificate attached to this affidavit or declaration.""
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13101(a)(3), California Probate Code, required affidavit statement of the 40-day elapse (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13101.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one state's specific waiting period for this specific no-court procedure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's estate, or that 40 days is a period used by any other state's comparable mechanism, where one exists.

WHAT THE AFFIDAVIT MUST STATE
Probate Code § 13101(a) lists what an affidavit or declaration under this procedure must state: the decedent's name; the date and place of death; that at least 40 days have elapsed since death, as shown by a certified copy of the death certificate attached to the affidavit; either that no California proceeding for administration of the estate is being or has been conducted, or that the personal representative has consented in writing to the transfer; the current gross fair market value of the decedent's California real and personal property (excluding § 13050 property), stated not to exceed the applicable statutory dollar amount; a description of the property sought; the name of the successor entitled to it; a statement that the affiant is that successor, or is authorized under § 13051 to act on the successor's behalf; a statement that no other person has a superior right to the property; a request that the property be paid, delivered, or transferred to the affiant; and a statement, made under penalty of perjury under California law, that the foregoing is true and correct.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) To collect money, receive tangible personal property, or have evidences of a debt, obligation, interest, right, security, or chose in action transferred under this chapter, an affidavit or a declaration under penalty of perjury under the laws of this state shall be furnished to the holder of the decedent's property stating all of the following: (1) The decedent's name. (2) The date and place of the decedent's death. (3) "At least 40 days have elapsed since the death of the decedent, as shown in a certified copy of the decedent's death certificate attached to this affidavit or declaration." (4) Either of the following, as appropriate: (A) "No proceeding is now being or has been conducted in California for administration of the decedent's estate." (B) "The decedent's personal representative has consented in writing to the payment, transfer, or delivery to the affiant or declarant of the property described in the affidavit or declaration." (5) "The current gross fair market value of the decedent's real and personal property in California, excluding the property described in Section 13050 of the California Probate Code and any property included in a petition filed under Section 13151 of the California Probate Code, does not exceed [Insert dollar amount specified in subdivision (g) of Section 13101 of the California Probate Code]." (6) A description of the property of the decedent that is to be paid, transferred, or delivered to the affiant or declarant. (7) The name of the successor of the decedent, as defined in Section 13006, to the described property. (8) Either of the following, as appropriate: (A) "The affiant or declarant is the successor of the decedent (as defined in Section 13006 of the California Probate Code) to the decedent's interest in the described property." (B) "The affiant or declarant is authorized under Section 13051 of the California Probate Code to act on behalf of the successor of the decedent (as defined in Section 13006 of the California Probate Code) with respect to the decedent's interest in the described property." (9) "No other person has a superior right to the interest of the decedent in the described property." (10) "The affiant or declarant requests that the described property be paid, delivered, or transferred to the affiant or declarant." (11) "The affiant or declarant affirms or declares under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct.""
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13101(a), California Probate Code, required contents of the small estate affidavit (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13101.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what one state's affidavit form must contain — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's estate, or that this exact list satisfies any other state's comparable procedure. This is a single statutory section (§ 13101); no additional independent source was found for this.

MULTIPLE SUCCESSORS AND THE ATTACHED DEATH CERTIFICATE
Where more than one person is entitled to the described property, Probate Code § 13101(b) requires the required statements to be modified to reflect that fact when each such person executes the affidavit or declaration — the statute contemplates joint execution by the interested successors rather than a single successor certifying on the others' behalf. Separately, § 13101(d) requires a certified copy of the decedent's death certificate to be attached to the affidavit or declaration.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(b) Where more than one person executes the affidavit or declaration under this section, the statements required by subdivision (a) shall be modified as appropriate to reflect that fact."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13101(b), California Probate Code, modification of statements for multiple successors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13101.)
  "(d) A certified copy of the decedent's death certificate shall be attached to the affidavit or declaration."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13101(d), California Probate Code, death certificate attachment requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13101.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one state's rule for multiple successors and required attachments — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's estate. This is a single statutory section (§ 13101); no additional independent source was found for this.

PROPERTY SCHEDULE
Schedule A — Property Described in This Affidavit: Checking account #1234 at Acme Bank; 2019 furniture and household items located at 123 Main St.

THE HOLDER'S DUTY TO HONOR THE AFFIDAVIT, AND ITS LIABILITY PROTECTION
Probate Code § 13106(a) provides that once the requirements of §§ 13100 to 13104 are satisfied, a holder of the decedent's property (such as a bank or transfer agent) who pays, delivers, or transfers property in reliance on the affidavit or declaration is discharged from any further liability with respect to that money or property — the holder may rely in good faith on the statements in the affidavit and has no duty to inquire into the truth of any of them. If a holder instead refuses to pay, deliver, or transfer the property to the successor within a reasonable time, Probate Code § 13105(b) lets the successor bring an action to recover the property or compel the transfer, and directs the court to award reasonable attorney's fees to the successor if it finds the holder acted unreasonably in refusing.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) If the requirements of Sections 13100 to 13104, inclusive, are satisfied, receipt by the holder of the decedent's property of the affidavit or declaration constitutes sufficient acquittance for the payment of money, delivery of property, or changing registered ownership of property pursuant to this chapter and discharges the holder from any further liability with respect to the money or property. The holder may rely in good faith on the statements in the affidavit or declaration and has no duty to inquire into the truth of any statement in the affidavit or declaration."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13106(a), California Probate Code, holder's discharge from liability (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13106.)
  "(b) If the holder of the decedent's property refuses to pay, deliver, or transfer any personal property or evidence thereof to the successor of the decedent within a reasonable time, the successor may recover the property or compel its payment, delivery, or transfer in an action brought for that purpose against the holder of the property. If an action is brought against the holder under this section, the court shall award reasonable attorney's fees to the person or persons bringing the action if the court finds that the holder of the decedent's property acted unreasonably in refusing to pay, deliver, or transfer the property to them as required by subdivision (a)."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13105(b), California Probate Code, successor's remedy for a holder's unreasonable refusal (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13105.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one state's rule protecting institutions that rely on this kind of affidavit — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's estate, or that a given institution outside California would treat an out-of-state equivalent the same way.

THE TRANSFEREE'S ONGOING LIABILITY FOR DEBTS AND SUPERIOR CLAIMS
Receiving property under this affidavit procedure does not clear the underlying debts or claims against Pat Morgan's estate. Probate Code § 13109 makes a transferee who receives property this way personally liable for Pat Morgan's unsecured debts, enforceable against the transferee the same way the debt could have been enforced against Pat Morgan, though that personal liability cannot exceed the fair market value of the transferred property, less any liens, at the time the affidavit was presented. Separately, Probate Code § 13111 lets a personal representative who later determines someone else has a superior right to the transferred property demand its return to the estate — restitution of the property itself, or, if the transferee no longer has it, its fair market value plus 7 percent annual interest — and, if the transferee obtained the property by fraud, restitution of three times its fair market value.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) A transferee is personally liable, to the extent provided in this section for the unsecured debts of the decedent. That debt may be enforced against the transferee in the same manner as it could have been enforced against the decedent if the decedent had not died. In any action based upon the debt, the transferee may assert any defense, cross-complaint, or setoff that would have been available to the decedent if the decedent had not died. Nothing in this section permits enforcement of a claim that is barred under Part 4 (commencing with Section 9000) of Division 7. Section 366.2 of the Code of Civil Procedure applies in an action under this section. (b) The personal liability under subdivision (a) shall not exceed the fair market value of the transferred property at the time the affidavit or declaration is presented under this chapter, less the amount of any liens and encumbrances on the transferred property at that time, and less the amount of any payment made pursuant to subdivision (a) of Section 13110."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13109(a)-(b), California Probate Code, transferee's personal liability for the decedent's unsecured debts (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13109.)
  "(a) If property is paid, delivered, or transferred to a transferee under this chapter, and the decedent's personal representative determines that another person has a superior right to the property by testate or intestate succession from the decedent, the personal representative may request that the transferred property be restored to the estate. Subject to subdivisions (b), (c), (d), (e), and (g) if the personal representative makes that request, the transferee is liable for all of the following: (1) If the transferee still has the transferred property, restitution of the transferred property to the decedent's estate. (2) If the transferee no longer has the transferred property, restitution to the decedent's estate of the fair market value of the transferred property plus interest from the date of disposition at the rate of 7 percent per annum on the fair market value of the transferred property. ... (b) Subject to subdivision (c) and subject to any additional liability the transferee has under Sections 13109 to 13113.5, inclusive, if the transferee fraudulently secured the payment, delivery, or transfer of the decedent's property under this chapter, the transferee is liable under this section for restitution of three times the fair market value of the transferred property."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13111(a)-(b), California Probate Code, restitution when another person has a superior right (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13111.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that one state's affidavit procedure does not itself discharge a recipient's exposure to the decedent's debts or to a person with a better claim — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's estate, or about what liability rules apply outside California.

THE SEPARATE REAL PROPERTY SMALL-VALUE AFFIDAVIT
California Probate Code § 13200 provides a second, distinct mechanism for small amounts of real property — separate from, and structured differently than, the personal-property affidavit procedure in §§ 13100-13106. No sooner than six months after the decedent's death, a successor may file an affidavit, on a Judicial Council form, in the superior court of the county where the decedent was domiciled (or, if not California-domiciled, where the real property is located), stating a legal description of the property, that funeral expenses, last-illness expenses, and all unsecured debts of the decedent have been paid, and that the property's gross value does not exceed the statutory ceiling for this chapter. Unlike the personal-property procedure — which involves no court filing at all — this affidavit must be accompanied by an inventory and appraisal of the real property made by a probate referee, and, once filed, the court clerk issues a certified copy that is recorded with the county recorder, indexed with the decedent as grantor and the successor as grantee. As last written into the statute's own text (effective January 1, 2020), the dollar ceiling recited in § 13200 is $55,425 for decedents who died before April 1, 2022; for deaths on or after that date, the statute points to the adjusted dollar amount separately published by the Judicial Council under § 890, without itself restating that current adjusted number in the code section's text — unlike § 13100/§ 13101, which were directly re-amended in 2024 to state $166,250.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) No sooner than six months from the death of a decedent, a person or persons claiming as successor of the decedent to a particular item of property that is real property may file in the superior court in the county in which the decedent was domiciled at the time of death, or if the decedent was not domiciled in this state at the time of death, then in any county in which real property of the decedent is located, an affidavit in the form prescribed by the Judicial Council pursuant to Section 1001 stating all of the following: (1) The name of the decedent. (2) The date and place of the decedent's death. (3) A legal description of the real property and the interest of the decedent therein. (4) The name and address of each person serving as guardian or conservator of the estate of the decedent at the time of the decedent's death, so far as known to the affiant. (5) "The gross value of all real property in the decedent's estate located in California, as shown by the inventory and appraisal attached to this affidavit, excluding the real property described in Section 13050 of the California Probate Code, does not exceed [Insert dollar amount specified in subdivision (h)]." (6) "At least six months have elapsed since the death of the decedent as shown in a certified copy of decedent's death certificate attached to this affidavit." (7) Either of the following, as appropriate: (A) "No proceeding is now being or has been conducted in California for administration of the decedent's estate." (B) "The decedent's personal representative has consented in writing to use of the procedure provided by this chapter." (8) "Funeral expenses, expenses of last illness, and all unsecured debts of the decedent have been paid." (9) "The affiant is the successor of the decedent (as defined in Section 13006 of the Probate Code) and to the decedent's interest in the described property, and no other person has a superior right to the interest of the decedent in the described property." (10) "The affiant declares under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct.""
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13200(a), California Probate Code, real property small-value affidavit — filing and required contents (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13200.)
  "(h) (1) When the decedent dies prior to April 1, 2022, the dollar amount for paragraph (5) of subdivision (a) is fifty-five thousand four hundred twenty-five dollars ($55,425). (2) When the decedent dies on or after April 1, 2022, the dollar amount for paragraph (5) of subdivision (a) is the adjusted dollar amount, published in accordance with subdivision (c) of Section 890, in effect on the date of the decedent's death."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13200(h), California Probate Code, real property small-value affidavit dollar ceiling (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13200.)
  "Upon receipt of the affidavit and the required fee, the court clerk, upon determining that the affidavit is complete and has the required attachments, shall file the affidavit and attachments and shall issue a certified copy of the affidavit without the attachments. The certified copy shall be recorded in the office of the county recorder of the county where the real property is located. The county recorder shall index the certified copy in the index of grantors and grantees. The decedent shall be indexed as the grantor and each person designated as a successor to the property in the certified copy shall be indexed as a grantee."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13202, California Probate Code, recording the real property small-value affidavit (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13202.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a second, separate, court-filing-based small-estate mechanism exists for real property alone — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's estate, and not a claim that $55,425 (as opposed to a later Judicial Council-published adjustment) is the number actually controlling on any particular date of death. Real-property small-estate procedures, where they exist at all, vary widely by state, and many states have no equivalent to this six-month, court-filed, real-property-only track. Two of these three citations (§ 13200(a) and § 13200(h)) are subsections of the same statutory section; no additional independent source was found for the dollar-ceiling text itself, though the recording step is separately confirmed at the genuinely independent § 13202.

SIGNATURE AND PERJURY DECLARATION
I affirm or declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct. Executed on May 10, 2026, at Sacramento, California.

☐ _________________________ Jordan Morgan, Affiant/Declarant

Probate Code § 13106(a) provides that once the requirements of §§ 13100 to 13104 are satisfied, a holder of the decedent's property (such as a bank or transfer agent) who pays, delivers, or transfers property in reliance on the affidavit or declaration is discharged from any further liability with respect to that money or property — the holder may rely in good faith on the statements in the affidavit and has no duty to inquire into the truth of any of them. If a holder instead refuses to pay, deliver, or transfer the property to the successor within a reasonable time, Probate Code § 13105(b) lets the successor bring an action to recover the property or compel the transfer, and directs the court to award reasonable attorney's fees to the successor if it finds the holder acted unreasonably in refusing.

Probate Code § 13109 makes a transferee who receives property this way personally liable for Pat Morgan's unsecured debts, enforceable against the transferee the same way the debt could have been enforced against Pat Morgan, though that personal liability cannot exceed the fair market value of the transferred property, less any liens, at the time the affidavit was presented. Separately, Probate Code § 13111 lets a personal representative who later determines someone else has a superior right to the transferred property demand its return to the estate — restitution of the property itself, or, if the transferee no longer has it, its fair market value plus 7 percent annual interest — and, if the transferee obtained the property by fraud, restitution of three times its fair market value.

citations.quote: (a) A transferee is personally liable, to the extent provided in this section for the unsecured debts of the decedent. That debt may be enforced against the transferee in the same manner as it could have been enforced against the decedent if the decedent had not died. In any action based upon the debt, the transferee may assert any defense, cross-complaint, or setoff that would have been available to the decedent if the decedent had not died. Nothing in this section permits enforcement of a claim that is barred under Part 4 (commencing with Section 9000) of Division 7. Section 366.2 of the Code of Civil Procedure applies in an action under this section. (b) The personal liability under subdivision (a) shall not exceed the fair market value of the transferred property at the time the affidavit or declaration is presented under this chapter, less the amount of any liens and encumbrances on the transferred property at that time, and less the amount of any payment made pursuant to subdivision (a) of Section 13110.

citations.quote: (a) If property is paid, delivered, or transferred to a transferee under this chapter, and the decedent's personal representative determines that another person has a superior right to the property by testate or intestate succession from the decedent, the personal representative may request that the transferred property be restored to the estate. Subject to subdivisions (b), (c), (d), (e), and (g) if the personal representative makes that request, the transferee is liable for all of the following: (1) If the transferee still has the transferred property, restitution of the transferred property to the decedent's estate. (2) If the transferee no longer has the transferred property, restitution to the decedent's estate of the fair market value of the transferred property plus interest from the date of disposition at the rate of 7 percent per annum on the fair market value of the transferred property. ... (b) Subject to subdivision (c) and subject to any additional liability the transferee has under Sections 13109 to 13113.5, inclusive, if the transferee fraudulently secured the payment, delivery, or transfer of the decedent's property under this chapter, the transferee is liable under this section for restitution of three times the fair market value of the transferred property.

expectedJSON.body: California Probate Code § 13200 provides a second, distinct mechanism for small amounts of real property — separate from, and structured differently than, the personal-property affidavit procedure in §§ 13100-13106. No sooner than six months after the decedent's death, a successor may file an affidavit, on a Judicial Council form, in the superior court of the county where the decedent was domiciled (or, if not California-domiciled, where the real property is located), stating a legal description of the property, that funeral expenses, last-illness expenses, and all unsecured debts of the decedent have been paid, and that the property's gross value does not exceed the statutory ceiling for this chapter. Unlike the personal-property procedure — which involves no court filing at all — this affidavit must be accompanied by an inventory and appraisal of the real property made by a probate referee, and, once filed, the court clerk issues a certified copy that is recorded with the county recorder, indexed with the decedent as grantor and the successor as grantee. As last written into the statute's own text (effective January 1, 2020), the dollar ceiling recited in § 13200 is $55,425 for decedents who died before April 1, 2022; for deaths on or after that date, the statute points to the adjusted dollar amount separately published by the Judicial Council under § 890, without itself restating that current adjusted number in the code section's text — unlike § 13100/§ 13101, which were directly re-amended in 2024 to state $166,250.

citations.cite: California Probate Code, real property small-value affidavit — filing and required contents
citations.quote: (a) No sooner than six months from the death of a decedent, a person or persons claiming as successor of the decedent to a particular item of property that is real property may file in the superior court in the county in which the decedent was domiciled at the time of death, or if the decedent was not domiciled in this state at the time of death, then in any county in which real property of the decedent is located, an affidavit in the form prescribed by the Judicial Council pursuant to Section 1001 stating all of the following: (1) The name of the decedent. (2) The date and place of the decedent's death. (3) A legal description of the real property and the interest of the decedent therein. (4) The name and address of each person serving as guardian or conservator of the estate of the decedent at the time of the decedent's death, so far as known to the affiant. (5) "The gross value of all real property in the decedent's estate located in California, as shown by the inventory and appraisal attached to this affidavit, excluding the real property described in Section 13050 of the California Probate Code, does not exceed [Insert dollar amount specified in subdivision (h)]." (6) "At least six months have elapsed since the death of the decedent as shown in a certified copy of decedent's death certificate attached to this affidavit." (7) Either of the following, as appropriate: (A) "No proceeding is now being or has been conducted in California for administration of the decedent's estate." (B) "The decedent's personal representative has consented in writing to use of the procedure provided by this chapter." (8) "Funeral expenses, expenses of last illness, and all unsecured debts of the decedent have been paid." (9) "The affiant is the successor of the decedent (as defined in Section 13006 of the Probate Code) and to the decedent's interest in the described property, and no other person has a superior right to the interest of the decedent in the described property." (10) "The affiant declares under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct."

citations.cite: California Probate Code, real property small-value affidavit dollar ceiling
citations.quote: (h) (1) When the decedent dies prior to April 1, 2022, the dollar amount for paragraph (5) of subdivision (a) is fifty-five thousand four hundred twenty-five dollars ($55,425). (2) When the decedent dies on or after April 1, 2022, the dollar amount for paragraph (5) of subdivision (a) is the adjusted dollar amount, published in accordance with subdivision (c) of Section 890, in effect on the date of the decedent's death.

citations.cite: California Probate Code, recording the real property small-value affidavit
citations.quote: Upon receipt of the affidavit and the required fee, the court clerk, upon determining that the affidavit is complete and has the required attachments, shall file the affidavit and attachments and shall issue a certified copy of the affidavit without the attachments. The certified copy shall be recorded in the office of the county recorder of the county where the real property is located. The county recorder shall index the certified copy in the index of grantors and grantees. The decedent shall be indexed as the grantor and each person designated as a successor to the property in the certified copy shall be indexed as a grantee.

Real-property small-estate procedures, where they exist at all, vary widely by state, and many states have no equivalent to this six-month, court-filed, real-property-only track. Two of these three citations (§ 13200(a) and § 13200(h)) are subsections of the same statutory section; no additional independent source was found for the dollar-ceiling text itself, though the recording step is separately confirmed at the genuinely independent § 13202.
